title: Permutation
body:
A **permutation** is an arrangement of things where **order matters**. Choosing $r$ items
from $n$ distinct items and caring which came first:

$$P(n, r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$

The reasoning is a product, not a formula to memorise. There are $n$ choices for the first
slot, $n-1$ for the second (one is used up), $n-2$ for the third, down to $n-r+1$ for the
last. Multiply them, and $n!/(n-r)!$ is just that product written compactly: the full
factorial with the tail you did not use divided back out.

Arranging **all** $n$ items is the special case $r = n$: $P(n, n) = n!/0! = n!$, which is
why $0! = 1$ is defined the way it is.

```
5 runners, how many ways to award gold, silver, bronze?
    order matters (gold ≠ bronze)
    P(5, 3) = 5!/2! = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60
```

## Versus combination

This is the only thing that gets confused, and the question to ask is always: **would
swapping two of the chosen items give a different outcome?**

| | Order matters | Formula | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permutation | yes | $\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ | podium places, passwords, seatings |
| [[Combination]] | no | $\dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$ | a committee, a poker hand, a subset |

$P(n, r)$ is always the larger of the two, by a factor of exactly $r!$: every combination
gets counted once for each of the $r!$ orders you could have picked it in.

## Variants

- **With repetition** (items can be reused, like a PIN): $n^r$, since every slot has all
  $n$ options again.
- **With repeated items** (arranging `MISSISSIPPI`): divide by the factorial of each
  repeat count, because swapping two identical letters is not a new arrangement.

## Why it matters for CS

Counting is how you size a search space before you try to search it. The reason a
[[Hamiltonian Cycle]] search is hopeless on anything large is that it is asking about
orderings of the vertices, and there are $n!$ of them, which grows faster than $2^n$.
Factorial-time brute force is the baseline that [[Asymptotic Analysis]] and
[[Time Complexity]] exist to improve on, and that [[NP-Complete]] exists to explain.

The other consumer is [[Probability]] in [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234). When outcomes are equally
likely a probability is $|A|/|S|$, so the whole problem becomes counting, and this note is the
numerator when order matters. The birthday problem is a permutation count divided by $365^n$.

## The other sense of the word

[[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) uses "permutation" for an **object** rather than a count: one
particular rearrangement, viewed as a bijection of a set to itself. Composing two of them gives a
third, so they form a [[Permutation Group]], and the largest one on $n$ symbols is the
[[Symmetric Group]] $S_n$.

The two senses meet at $n!$. Here it is the answer to "how many orderings of $n$ things"; there it
is $|S_n|$, the size of that group. Same number, one counted and one measured, and the
$\Omega(n\log n)$ sorting bound in [[Sequential Sorting]] uses it in the first sense while
[[Lagrange's Theorem]] uses it in the second.

Both senses are used at once, on the same object, in exactly one place in the vault: a
[[Transposition Cipher]] in [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111) has a permutation as its key. The
cryptanalyst wants the count, $m!$, to know how much searching that is; the algebraist wants the
structure, because the decryption key is the inverse permutation.
